# The Museum of Rain That Never Fell

The museum occupied the oldest house on Vey’s hill, a narrow stone building with blue windows and a roof stained green by decades of weather. Its official name was the Municipal Archive of Atmospheric Possibility. Everyone in town called it the weather museum.

Downstairs, behind three locks and a door swollen by damp, twelve thousand glass bottles stood on oak shelves. Some were the size of medicine bottles. Others reached from the floor to the ceiling and contained entire clouds, compressed into silver ropes and pale, luminous knots. Each had a paper label tied around its neck with string.

Edda’s first task of the morning was to dust the bottles.

“The rain that arrived after the bridge burned, so everyone came home by the river,” she read from one label. She drew a soft brush across the glass. “The snow that covered Vey on the night the school bell rang by itself. Fog on the morning after the funeral, when nobody could see the road. Hail that dented every apple in the eastern orchards, then restored them overnight.”

“The restoring apples are nonsense,” said Pell, carrying an empty crate.

“Someone remembered them very clearly.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“That is the sort of argument that gets young people hired,” Edda replied, though she smiled.

Pell was seventeen, all elbows and enthusiasm, and had begun his apprenticeship at the museum that spring. He wanted to study rivers, preferably by living beside one. The job required him to clean shelves, sharpen pencils, and never touch a stopper without permission. He had already touched three.

The weather museum had been founded by Edda’s grandfather, who had believed that every place needed an official record of what might have been. A town remembered its floods, fires, and victories. Why, he wondered, should it preserve the hailstorm that might have destroyed the harvest but left the beehives unharmed? Why should the school bell ring only for the birthdays of children who grew up lonely? A storm carried more than rain. It carried all the lives that might have branched beneath it.

Edda’s mother, Lisbet, had directed the museum for thirty years. She had written labels in her small, precise hand and taught Edda to read pressure changes in the sky. She had also possessed the peculiar talent of knowing when a visitor was lying about why they had come.

The last bottle Lisbet had catalogued contained thunder.

Edda remembered the night it arrived. She was twenty-three, working late while thunderstorms rolled in from the mountains. A stranger brought the bottle through the door, sodden and wild-eyed, saying he had caught it beneath the old bell tower. Lisbet had listened to the storm inside it, one hand pressed against the glass.

“What day is it for?” she had asked.

“My daughter’s wedding.”

Lisbet had frowned. “Weddings don’t call for this much thunder.”

“He’s afraid it will rain.”

Edda had left before the argument continued. Three days later, Tomas, Edda’s younger brother, walked into the same storm and did not return. Searchers found his red scarf snagged on a thorn bush above the river. They found his boot near the reservoir, though not his body. The thunder bottle remained in the archive, blankly labeled, waiting for a description no one could agree upon.

After Lisbet died, the town appointed Havel as the museum’s new director.

He arrived on a bright morning with a suitcase, a grant proposal, and a chart showing Vey’s rainfall over the past hundred years. “The winters are wetter,” he said, spreading the chart across Edda’s desk. “The summers are less reliable. We need a plan.”

“We have records.”

“Records don’t keep the sun shining.”

On his first day, Havel had the lower windows painted white and arranged bottles of condensation along his office wall. He was broad-shouldered and careful with his shoes, a man who had grown up somewhere larger and was still learning the dimensions of Vey. He asked thoughtful questions. He listened when people spoke. And beneath all that, Edda sensed a terrible impatience, as though he were waiting for a train everyone else had missed.

Pell admired him.

“He says the museum could make weather,” the boy whispered one afternoon. “Not predict it. Make it.”

“That would be quite a change from dusting.”

“The town would never be cold again.”

“The town would never be surprised again.”

Pell considered this. “Maybe that isn’t such a bad thing.”

Edda looked at him sharply, but he was examining a jar of golden dust. He did not notice her expression.

The first visitor to arrive after Havel’s appointment was an old woman named Lenka. She walked uphill slowly, pausing at every stone wall, carrying a small brown case. Havel welcomed her with tea and asked what atmospheric curiosity brought her to the archive.

“I want the fog,” Lenka said.

Edda’s hand stopped above the catalogue.

“The morning I met my husband,” Lenka continued. “It was foggy. I was eleven. He was the bus driver.”

Havel opened the town registry. “There are thirty-one recorded fogs from your childhood. We would need the date.”

“I don’t know the date.”

“Perhaps the year?”

“I know the year.”

“Then we can make an educated guess.”

Lenka shook her head. “He gave me his scarf because the bus heater was broken. The fog came over the river. We talked until it burned my shoes. I’d like to see it again.”

Havel promised to review the records, but Edda knew what she would find. The weather museum preserved storms, not individual moments. Its labels described possibilities at the scale of a town, a season, a lifetime. It could hold the thunder before a wedding. It could hold the silence after a death.

It could not bring back the smell of a bus heater burning.

After Lenka left, Havel studied Edda across the desk. “You could find it. With the right equipment.”

“Finding it isn’t the same as having it.”

“Everything in that building is a piece of weather someone wished they could keep.”

“Not everyone’s wishes are the museum’s business.”

Havel’s eyes softened. “No. Only the ones powerful enough to make us look.”

That evening, Edda stayed late to finish an inventory. The archive was quiet except for the bottles settling on their shelves. Inside them, trapped currents made tiny ticking sounds, like clocks in a dozen different rooms. She loved those sounds. As a child, she had believed they were the museum breathing in its sleep.

Tomas used to say the bottles were full of doors.

“What kind?” she had asked.

“The kind that open when you’re ready,” he had replied, never explaining further.

She had been angry with him the night he disappeared. They had argued over his plan to work on the mountain observatory. She had said, “You’re always leaving.” He had said, “That isn’t true.” She had said, “Then stay and prove it.” He had gone anyway.

Havel found her beside the unlabelled thunder bottle.

He told her what he had learned from the old registers. Lisbet had been experimenting with a process she called gathering: drawing the pressure from one storm and moving it elsewhere. Havel had seen the notes. The process was unfinished, but a working model lay in the basement, built from copper coils and glass valves.

“She thought she could protect the valley,” he said.

“From what?”

“From the weather she was most afraid of.”

Edda pictured her mother bent over her instruments, her face illuminated by lightning. She saw Tomas climbing toward the reservoir, his red scarf bright against the black trees.

“She knew he was up there.”

“She knew there was a storm.”

“You don’t answer a question by changing the subject.”

“She did answer it. That’s why she stopped working.”

Havel reached into his coat and produced a key. It was warm, as though it had been held near a flame.

“Your mother’s laboratory,” he said.

Edda took the key but did not use it. Instead, she went back to dusting the bottles. The thunder inside its jar rolled from one side to the other.

Pell found the laboratory on his own.

He came running into the lower archive the next morning, his face pale beneath its dusty tan. “Edda,” he called. “I found her notebook.”

In the garden shed, behind a stack of cracked flowerpots, lay a wooden box containing hundreds of narrow pages. Pell had carried them to the museum in his shirt. The diagrams were intricate: arrows of air, spirals of pressure, the mathematics of storms. Some pages were dated. Others were written in a hurry.

One passage had been underlined three times: *Weather is memory given permission to move.*

Another read: *There are worse outcomes than rain.*

The final page contained only a list of names. Tomas’s was near the bottom, followed by a question mark.

Edda sat on the floor among the flowerpots and read it twice.

“She knew he might die,” Pell said quietly.

“She knew the storm was dangerous.”

“She gathered it anyway.”

“She was afraid.”

“Does that change what she did?”

Edda folded the page. “Ask her.”

But her mother had been dead for two years, and questions were easier to carry than answers.

The council approved Havel’s grant six days later. Vey would become the first town in the region to manufacture its own climate. The old museum would remain open to visitors, but its bottles would be connected to the new machinery. Havel promised fair winters, mild summers, and a steady supply of rain for the farms. He spoke about freedom from disaster as if it were simply another civic amenity.

The machinery was installed beneath the eastern wall. Copper pipes climbed through the old stonework and disappeared into the roof. On the first day of testing, the pumps produced a fragrant green haze. It smelled of crushed pine and rain-soaked grass.

Havel stood before the townspeople with his hands behind his back. “We can improve upon nature,” he said. “Or at least negotiate with it.”

Applause began uncertainly. A few people looked at one another. Others studied the sky.

Edda watched a bottle of thunder tremble on its shelf.

That night, she finally used Lisbet’s key.

The laboratory was smaller than she remembered. Glass tubes crossed the ceiling like vines. A chair stood before a circular window, its back still tilted toward the moon. On the workbench lay a row of labeled jars: spring rain, early frost, thunder over a wheat field, a summer wind that carried smoke from distant fires.

Each jar was nearly empty.

“She used them for experiments,” Edda said.

“Or for the gathering process,” Havel replied. He had followed her downstairs, footsteps deliberate on the wooden stairs. “She was trying to make Vey safe.”

“She made it quiet.”

“That isn’t the same as safe.”

“Yes. It is.”

Havel sat on the edge of the workbench. In the green light, he looked older. “I lost my son to a flood,” he said. “Twenty years ago. He was nine. The water came through a wall everyone had said was solid.”

Edda looked away.

“I thought if I could control the weather, I could promise someone else they would never lose what I lost.” He touched one of the empty jars. “Your mother understood. That’s why I came here.”

“Because she found a way to bring him back.”

“No. Because she found a way to stop blaming the sky.”

The word *blaming* irritated her, but she had no answer for it. Outside, the machinery hummed. Through the laboratory window, she could see clouds assembling above the hills, thin and deliberate as rows of cotton.

The next morning, Pell was waiting for her beside the thunder bottle.

Edda had told him never to touch a stopper, but he had removed the entire neck of the glass. He held it in both hands, and the bottle poured a dark storm onto the floor.

Thunder shook the cups from their hooks.

Rain fell upward, striking the ceiling and streaming toward the shelves. The labels lifted from their strings and whirled around the room like pale leaves. The smell of the mountain entered through the cracks in the walls: pine, wet stone, cold metal.

Then the room filled with voices.

Not words, exactly. Sounds arrived in fragments. A kettle beginning to whistle. A shoe scraping a floor. Someone laughing with their mouth full. A woman saying *Tomas*, in Lisbet’s voice, calling his name from very far away.

Edda dropped to her knees.

In the storm she saw herself as a child, hiding beneath the kitchen table. She saw her mother at the door, reaching for a coat. She saw Tomas running down the stairs, a paper boat in his hand. She saw the instant before he turned toward the hill.

The memory was not a punishment. It was a room in which she had lived for years without entering.

Havel pulled the bottle from Pell’s hands. “Stop it.”

“He’s in there,” Edda whispered. “He’s still in there.”

“He isn’t.”

“I can hear him.”

Havel seized her shoulders. “You are hearing what you need to hear. That is what weather does.”

The storm struck again. Lightning illuminated the room white. In its flash, Edda saw the place where she had been all her life: the chair at the kitchen table, the empty bed next to her brother’s, the door she had closed after an argument because closing it felt more powerful than opening it.

She had spent years believing that if she could find the right bottle, the right day, the right kind of rain, she could go back.

She could not.

Lenka was waiting outside the laboratory.

The old woman had climbed the hill again, carrying her brown case. Behind her stood a handful of townspeople, drawn by the storm and the strange lights in the museum windows. They had brought their own bottles. A baker held a jar of summer lightning. The schoolteacher carried the snowfall from the night the river froze. Someone had brought a bottle labeled simply: *Rain on the day the mine closed, and everyone forgave everyone else.*

Lenka lifted the case. “I found something,” she said.

Inside lay a blue glass bead.

“My husband gave it to me,” she said. “He said the fog made it from the river. I don’t know whether that was true. I’ve carried it since I was eleven.”

Edda looked at the bead. It was clouded with age, lovely and useless.

“I remember the fog,” Lenka said. “Maybe that is enough.”

Havel looked toward the laboratory. “The bottles are connected to the machinery. If we open them now, the gathering process could spread.”

“Then disconnect them.”

“There isn’t time.”

“There’s never enough time for the right thing,” Edda said. “That’s why people build museums.”

The machines beneath the eastern wall began to sing. Their pitch rose as the bottles rattled on their shelves. Vey’s manufactured spring thundered through the pipes, hungry for the real storm overhead.

Edda took the stopper from the unlabelled bottle.

She did not release the thunder into the machinery. She climbed the ladder to the cupola, carrying the bottle against her chest. Havel followed her, shouting for her to wait. Pell followed Havel. Below them, the townspeople gathered at the foot of the tower, clutching their jars and their memories.

The roof opened beneath a round glass window. Above it waited a sky crowded with impossible weather. Clouds of every size hung over the hills. Rain fell in silver curtains. Lightning branched between them. A faint sun shone through one gap, not conquering the darkness but making it more visible.

Edda lifted the bottle.

“Wait!” Havel grabbed her arm. “You don’t know what will happen.”

“No,” she said. “That’s the point.”

She emptied the thunder into the night.

The storm rose.

For a moment, it formed a column above the museum, turning the rain and hail and frozen moonlight upward. Bottles cracked on their shelves. Glass, string, and paper swirled through the air. The tower shook hard enough to make the crowd cry out.

Then the weather broke apart.

It fell over Vey as rain, snow, fog, wind, and brilliant sunlight all at once. The roofs shone. The streets gleamed. Every window in the town reflected a different sky. Somewhere below, a child laughed because it was snowing in midsummer. Somewhere else, a woman wept because the rain sounded like applause.

Lenka opened her blue bead. Fog drifted from it, gentle as breath, and spread across the hill. In that fog, the old woman saw a bus at the river bend. She saw a young driver with red gloves. She saw the boy she had spoken to for eleven minutes, while the world around them disappeared.

He looked at her and smiled.

Lenka placed her hand over her heart.

The townspeople began opening their bottles.

The baker released the lightning, and sparks skipped along the cobblestones. The schoolteacher opened the snowfall, and the hill became white beneath the summer stars. People called to one another across the storm. They held up labels. They laughed, argued, forgave, and wept. Weather that had waited years for permission to fall finally found the ground.

Havel climbed onto the roof beside Edda.

His face was wet. He could not have said whether the rain or the fog had reached him first. Below, the machinery groaned as the gathered storms poured through its copper veins. The laboratory window burst outward. A long tongue of flame licked across the tiles and vanished into the sky.

“We could lose the museum,” he said.

“No,” Edda replied. “Not this one.”

The unlabelled bottle lay empty at her feet. She picked it up anyway. There was no thunder inside it now. No voice. No glimpse of her brother returning along a mountain road. The glass held only the reflection of the sky: imperfect, moving, alive.

By morning, the storm had passed.

Snow covered the hill. The weather machinery lay in pieces, its copper pipes twisted into shapes that resembled vines, reeds, and question marks. The museum’s roof had a hole, but the old walls stood. Most of the bottles survived. Many were empty. A few still held clouds, though these were ordinary clouds, soft with snow and almost gentle.

Edda found Lisbet’s notebook in the snow.

The final page had been blank beneath the list of names. Edda took a pencil from her pocket. For a long time, she considered writing an explanation: *The day my mother gathered a storm instead of searching for my brother.* She considered another: *The day I learned that fear can imitate love, and safety can become a prison.*

She wrote neither.

Instead, she wrote: **Weather of a day I did not know how to name.**

Then she carried the notebook inside.

Havel stayed in Vey. He did not rebuild the machinery. He redesigned the museum’s upper room as a classroom and began teaching residents to read clouds without assuming they could command them. His forecasts became famous for their honesty. “Probably rain,” he would say. “Possibly hail. We have no idea what the mountains are thinking.”

Pell kept working at the museum. He learned to repair the bottles and eventually to make new ones. He stopped insisting that ordinary records were worthless. One spring, he opened a museum of rivers on the coast, but he returned often to Vey, where he claimed the weather was more interesting.

Lenka visited the fog room every morning.

She never asked to meet her husband again. She said she had remembered what mattered: his hands around the steering wheel, the sound of rain on the bus roof, and the moment when he had asked her name and made her feel, for the first time, as though she might be worth knowing.

Edda painted the empty bottles white.

On the old thunder bottle, she left a new label. The string hung loose. The words were faint beneath the winter light.

*Returned.*

The museum reopened on a cloudy afternoon, just before sunset. Visitors came in with muddy boots and questions. They asked whether the town had really experienced a thunderstorm in July, and whether the river had frozen beneath a burning sky, and whether it was true that the baker’s lightning had made every apple in the eastern orchards glow.

“We can show you the records,” Edda would answer, “but we can’t promise they happened.”

“What are records for, then?” a child asked.

“To remind us that being remembered is not the same as being unchanged.”

She had once hated explanations. She had grown tired of them now. Some things could be entered without being announced. A cup set down beside someone you loved. Rain beginning on a roof. A voice calling from the other room, only to ask whether you had eaten.

At closing time, she climbed the hill alone.

The old museum stood beneath the evening sky, its blue windows lit from within. Somewhere inside, Pell was counting bottles. Havel was arguing cheerfully with the schoolteacher. The machinery had been replaced by a long wooden table, and on the table lay cups, notebooks, and a plate of pastries nobody had remembered to finish.

Edda stood on the hill and listened.

The town made its own weather now.

It was not always gentle. It was not always bright. It arrived without permission, carrying what it pleased, changing the color of the roofs, bending the trees, making the roads shine. It could destroy a harvest. It could fill a cemetery with flowers. It could bring a stranger home at exactly the right moment, or not.

Edda had once believed that safety meant closing every door. She understood now that a door could be opened without knowing what waited beyond it. That was why they built the museum. Not to keep the world still, but to make room for wonder when the world insisted on moving.

The clouds gathered over the mountains, dark and silver and full of unnamed weather.

Edda smiled.

Whatever happened next, she would let it come.

In the storm she saw herself as a child, hiding beneath the kitchen table. She saw her mother at the door, reaching for a coat. She saw Tomas running down the stairs, a paper boat in his hand. She saw the instant before he turned toward the hill.

The memory was not a punishment. It was a room in which she had lived for years without entering.

Havel pulled the bottle from Pell’s hands. “Stop it.”

“He’s in there,” Edda whispered. “He’s still in there.”

“He isn’t.”

“I can hear him.”

Havel seized her shoulders. “You are hearing what you need to hear. That is what weather does.”

The storm struck again. Lightning illuminated the room white. In its flash, Edda saw the place where she had been all her life: the chair at the kitchen table, the empty bed next to her brother’s, the door she had closed after an argument because closing it felt more powerful than opening it.

She had spent years believing that if she could find the right bottle, the right day, the right kind of rain, she could go back.

She could not.

Lenka was waiting outside the laboratory.

The old woman had climbed the hill again, carrying her brown case. Behind her stood a handful of townspeople, drawn by the storm and the strange lights in the museum windows. They had brought their own bottles. A baker held a jar of summer lightning. The schoolteacher carried the snowfall from the night the river froze. Someone had brought a bottle labeled simply: *Rain on the day the mine closed, and everyone forgave everyone else.*

Lenka lifted the case. “I found something,” she said.

Inside lay a blue glass bead.

“My husband gave it to me,” she said. “He said the fog made it from the river. I don’t know whether that was true. I’ve carried it since I was eleven.”

Edda looked at the bead. It was clouded with age, lovely and useless.

“I remember the fog,” Lenka said. “Maybe that is enough.”

Havel looked toward the laboratory. “The bottles are connected to the machinery. If we open them now, the gathering process could spread.”

“Then disconnect them.”

“There isn’t time.”

“There’s never enough time for the right thing,” Edda said. “That’s why people build museums.”

The machines beneath the eastern wall began to sing. Their pitch rose as the bottles rattled on their shelves. Vey’s manufactured spring thundered through the pipes, hungry for the real storm overhead.

Edda took the stopper from the unlabelled bottle.

She did not release the thunder into the machinery. She climbed the ladder to the cupola, carrying the bottle against her chest. Havel followed her, shouting for her to wait. Pell followed Havel. Below them, the townspeople gathered at the foot of the tower, clutching their jars and their memories.

The roof opened beneath a round glass window. Above it waited a sky crowded with impossible weather. Clouds of every size hung over the hills. Rain fell in silver curtains. Lightning branched between them. A faint sun shone through one gap, not conquering the darkness but making it more visible.

Edda lifted the bottle.

“Wait!” Havel grabbed her arm. “You don’t know what will happen.”

“No,” she said. “That’s the point.”

She emptied the thunder into the night.

The storm rose.

For a moment, it formed a column above the museum, turning the rain and hail and frozen moonlight upward. Bottles cracked on their shelves. Glass, string, and paper swirled through the air. The tower shook hard enough to make the crowd cry out.

Then the weather broke apart.

It fell over Vey as rain, snow, fog, wind, and brilliant sunlight all at once. The roofs shone. The streets gleamed. Every window in the town reflected a different sky. Somewhere below, a child laughed because it was snowing in midsummer. Somewhere else, a woman wept because the rain sounded like applause.

Lenka opened her blue bead. Fog drifted from it, gentle as breath, and spread across the hill. In that fog, the old woman saw a bus at the river bend. She saw a young driver with red gloves. She saw the boy she had spoken to for eleven minutes, while the world around them disappeared.

He looked at her and smiled.

Lenka placed her hand over her heart.

The townspeople began opening their bottles.

The baker released the lightning, and sparks skipped along the cobblestones. The schoolteacher opened the snowfall, and the hill became white beneath the summer stars. People called to one another across the storm. They held up labels. They laughed, argued, forgave, and wept. Weather that had waited years for permission to fall finally found the ground.

Havel climbed onto the roof beside Edda.

His face was wet. He could not have said whether the rain or the fog had reached him first. Below, the machinery groaned as the gathered storms poured through its copper veins. The laboratory window burst outward. A long tongue of flame licked across the tiles and vanished into the sky.

“We could lose the museum,” he said.

“No,” Edda replied. “Not this one.”

The unlabelled bottle lay empty at her feet. She picked it up anyway. There was no thunder inside it now. No voice. No glimpse of her brother returning along a mountain road. The glass held only the reflection of the sky: imperfect, moving, alive.

By morning, the storm had passed.

Snow covered the hill. The weather machinery lay in pieces, its copper pipes twisted into shapes that resembled vines, reeds, and question marks. The museum’s roof had a hole, but the old walls stood. Most of the bottles survived. Many were empty. A few still held clouds, though these were ordinary clouds, soft with snow and almost gentle.

Edda found Lisbet’s notebook in the snow.

The final page had been blank beneath the list of names. Edda took a pencil from her pocket. For a long time, she considered writing an explanation: *The day my mother gathered a storm instead of searching for my brother.* She considered another: *The day I learned that fear can imitate love, and safety can become a prison.*

She wrote neither.

Instead, she wrote: **Weather of a day I did not know how to name.**

Then she carried the notebook inside.

Havel stayed in Vey. He did not rebuild the machinery. He redesigned the museum’s upper room as a classroom and began teaching residents to read clouds without assuming they could command them. His forecasts became famous for their honesty. “Probably rain,” he would say. “Possibly hail. We have no idea what the mountains are thinking.”

Pell kept working at the museum. He learned to repair the bottles and eventually to make new ones. He stopped insisting that ordinary records were worthless. One spring, he opened a museum of rivers on the coast, but he returned often to Vey, where he claimed the weather was more interesting.

Lenka visited the fog room every morning.

She never asked to meet her husband again. She said she had remembered what mattered: his hands around the steering wheel, the sound of rain on the bus roof, and the moment when he had asked her name and made her feel, for the first time, as though she might be worth knowing.

Edda painted the empty bottles white.

On the old thunder bottle, she left a new label. The string hung loose. The words were faint beneath the winter light.

*Returned.*

The museum reopened on a cloudy afternoon, just before sunset. Visitors came in with muddy boots and questions. They asked whether the town had really experienced a thunderstorm in July, and whether the river had frozen beneath a burning sky, and whether it was true that the baker’s lightning had made every apple in the eastern orchards glow.

“We can show you the records,” Edda would answer, “but we can’t promise they happened.”

“What are records for, then?” a child asked.

“To remind us that being remembered is not the same as being unchanged.”

She had once hated explanations. She had grown tired of them now. Some things could be entered without being announced. A cup set down beside someone you loved. Rain beginning on a roof. A voice calling from the other room, only to ask whether you had eaten.

At closing time, she climbed the hill alone.

The old museum stood beneath the evening sky, its blue windows lit from within. Somewhere inside, Pell was counting bottles. Havel was arguing cheerfully with the schoolteacher. The machinery had been replaced by a long wooden table, and on the table lay cups, notebooks, and a plate of pastries nobody had remembered to finish.

Edda stood on the hill and listened.

The town made its own weather now.

It was not always gentle. It was not always bright. It arrived without permission, carrying what it pleased, changing the color of the roofs, bending the trees, making the roads shine. It could destroy a harvest. It could fill a cemetery with flowers. It could bring a stranger home at exactly the right moment, or not.

Edda had once believed that safety meant closing every door. She understood now that a door could be opened without knowing what waited beyond it. That was why they built the museum. Not to keep the world still, but to make room for wonder when the world insisted on moving.

The clouds gathered over the mountains, dark and silver and full of unnamed weather.

Edda smiled.

Whatever happened next, she would let it come.
